data.reference_solution:
def mergeTwoLists(list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    vals = []
    curr = list1
    while curr:
        vals.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    curr = list2
    while curr:
        vals.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    vals.sort()
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    for v in vals:
        curr.next = ListNode(v)
        curr = curr.next
    return dummy.next
data.generator_code:
def _list_to_node(lst):
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    for val in lst:
        curr.next = ListNode(val)
        curr = curr.next
    return dummy.next

def generate(rng, n):
    n1 = rng.randint(0, n)
    n2 = rng.randint(0, n)
    l1 = sorted([rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(n1)])
    l2 = sorted([rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(n2)])
    return [_list_to_node(l1), _list_to_node(l2)]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    l1 = sorted([rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(n)])
    l2 = sorted([rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(n)])
    return [_list_to_node(l1), _list_to_node(l2)]

data.key_insight: Using a dummy head node simplifies the edge cases of appending to an empty list, allowing us to build the merged list seamlessly by comparing the front of both lists.

steps.title: Initialize Dummy Head
steps.detail: Create a dummy ListNode and a current pointer to track the tail of the new merged list.

steps.title: Iterate and Compare
steps.detail: While both list1 and list2 are non-empty, compare their front values. Attach the smaller node to the current pointer and advance that list's pointer.

steps.title: Attach Remaining Nodes
steps.detail: Once one of the lists is exhausted, attach the remaining part of the other list directly to the end of the merged list.

steps.title: Return Result
steps.detail: Return dummy.next, which points to the actual head of the merged sorted list.

data.pattern_summary: Use two pointers moving independently across separate inputs to compare or combine elements in linear time.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We can maintain one pointer in each list to compare their current elements and build the result in order.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Storing frequencies or values in a hash map ignores the pre-existing sorted order of the inputs and adds unnecessary overhead.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window is used for contiguous subarrays or sublists of a fixed size, not for merging two distinct collections.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While the lists are sorted, binary search is for finding elements, not for sequentially merging two full lists.

signals.phrase: Two sorted linked lists list1 and list2
signals.hint: Having two separate inputs that are already ordered suggests we should traverse them simultaneously.
We can build the final sorted sequence on the fly by always picking the smaller of the two current front elements.

data.brute_force_idea: Traverse both linked lists to collect all their integer values into a Python list, sort that list, and then construct a brand new linked list from the sorted values.
data.brute_force_why: We visit every node to extract values, which takes O(N) time, but then sorting all collected elements takes O(N log N) time.
data.bottleneck: Sorting the collected values discards the fact that the input lists were already sorted, forcing an O(N log N) time complexity instead of O(N).
bottleneck_hints: Look at how the input lists are initially given to you.
Notice that you are gathering all elements into an array and then sorting them from scratch.
Ask yourself if you actually need to sort the elements after collecting them, or if you could compare the front elements of the lists directly.
data.brute_force_code:
def mergeTwoLists(list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    vals = []
    curr = list1
    while curr:
        vals.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    curr = list2
    while curr:
        vals.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    vals.sort()
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    for v in vals:
        curr.next = ListNode(v)
        curr = curr.next
    return dummy.next

data.overview: The mergeTwoLists algorithm combines two sorted linked lists into a single sorted list by maintaining a pointer to the smaller front element at each step. Using a dummy head node allows us to seamlessly build the new list without special casing the start.
data.intuition: Imagine two lines of people already sorted by height, merging into a single line. At each step, you look at the two people at the front of each line, pick the shorter one, and add them to your new combined line.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The optimized solution removes the bottleneck of extracting and sorting all values by building the new list on the fly. Because both input lists are already sorted, we can compare their front elements at each step and attach the smaller one directly to our result pointer. This processes every node exactly once without allocating an extra array or sorting.

derivation.note: The while loop runs until either list1 or list2 runs out of nodes.
Performs a comparison between the current heads of both lists.
Attaches a node from list1 when it is smaller or equal.
Attaches a node from list2 when it is smaller.
Checks if any nodes remain in list1 after the loop finishes.
Attaches the remaining nodes from list2 if list1 finished first.

data.time_summary: Lines 6 through 13 dominate the execution, running proportionally to the total number of nodes across both lists. The leftover attachment checks take constant time. Thus, the total time complexity is O(n + m).
data.space_summary: The solution only creates a single dummy node and a few pointer variables, reusing the existing nodes from the input lists rather than duplicating them. Thus, the auxiliary space complexity is O(1).
data.takeaway: When merging two already sorted sequences, use a two-pointer approach to select the next element in linear time instead of collecting and sorting everything.
mistakes: Forgetting to advance the pointer of the list you just pulled a node from, creating an infinite loop.
Returning the dummy node itself instead of dummy.next, which returns the placeholder rather than the actual head of the merged list.
Failing to attach the remaining tail of whichever list still has nodes after the main while loop terminates.
